entities.name: Greek Orthodoxy
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Greek Orthodox Church (Patriarchate of Constantinople — the Ecumenical Patriarchate) represents the oldest continuous Christian episcopal see and the spiritual center of Eastern Orthodox Christianity's 220 million worldwide adherents. The Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople holds the primacy of honor (but not jurisdiction) over 14 autocephalous Orthodox churches — maintaining continuity with the Christian communities of Byzantium, the Great Schism of 1054 that split Eastern and Western Christianity, and the Byzantine Empire's 1,000-year theological tradition.

Constantinople's Bishop claimed primacy in the Christian East from the Council of Constantinople (381 CE), which ranked the 'New Rome' above Alexandria and Antioch. The Ecumenical Patriarchate survived the Ottoman conquest of 1453 — Sultan Mehmed II deliberately preserved Patriarch Gennadios as leader of the Greek-speaking Christian community (millet) rather than risk Christian holy sites becoming political grievances. The Patriarchate operated from the Phanar (Fener) district of Istanbul under Ottoman authority for 469 years.

The Great Schism of 1054 — the mutual excommunication of Pope Leo IX's legate and Patriarch Michael Cerularius over the filioque clause (whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from Father and Son) — divided Christianity's two great traditions permanently. Byzantine theology's influence on Renaissance humanism (via émigré scholars fleeing Ottoman conquest after 1453), Orthodox missions to the Slavic world (Saints Cyril and Methodius creating the Cyrillic alphabet), and the Hesychast controversy (Gregory Palamas's theology of divine light) define Orthodoxy's intellectual contributions.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Greek Orthodox Church's Great Schism of 1054 — splitting Christendom's two great traditions — and Cyrillic alphabet creation for Slavic peoples are among Christianity's most consequential institutional moments, shaping 220 million believers and 12 nations' writing systems.
